Package io.mavlink4j.service

Class ParameterService

java.lang.Object
io.mavlink4j.service.ParameterService
public final class ParameterService extends Object
MAVLink's parameter microservice (parameter protocol): read a named parameter, and write one with a mandatory read-back. Family A, so the retry/deadline mechanics come from RequestResponse; this class supplies only Parameter's own policy — how a name becomes a MatchKey, and what counts as a satisfying reply.

Read by name, never by index

PARAM_REQUEST_READ can address a parameter either by param_id or by param_index. This service always sends the name with READ_BY_NAME in the index field, because a parameter's index is a property of one firmware build's table and shifts between versions — an index read is a correct-looking way to read the wrong parameter after an update.

A write is a read-back, not a send

write(io.mavlink4j.PeerId, java.lang.String, float, io.dronefleet.mavlink.common.MavParamType) is not fire-and-forget and has no fire-and-forget variant. An autopilot answers PARAM_SET with a PARAM_VALUE carrying what it actually stored, which is not always what was asked: out-of-range values are clamped and a float lands in whatever integer width the parameter really is. So the exchange completes with ParameterOutcome.Status.MISMATCH unless the echoed value is bit-for-bit what was requested. This is what makes a write safely reportable to an operator ("yes, with before/after values").

How a 16-character name fits in a 64-bit discriminator

It does not — CorrelationKeys hashes the name to route the reply, and this class verifies it by exact string compare on arrival. A PARAM_VALUE that lands on our key but names a different parameter is therefore not accepted: the classifier keeps the same waiter alive for another window rather than resending, bounded by MavlinkSettings.Parameter.maxForeignReplies() so a pathological stream cannot wedge the caller's future. That bound exists for completeness, not for a case anyone expects to see — an FNV-1a 64 collision between two ≤16-character parameter names is not something a fleet will encounter.

Non-goal: the full parameter download

PARAM_REQUEST_LIST — the "stream me all ~1200 parameters" protocol, with its own missing-index gap detection and re-request loop — is deliberately not implemented. Typical host needs (probe, readiness checks, remediation) address a short list of parameters it can name in advance, and a full download on a 2.4 kB/s telemetry link costs minutes of airtime.

  • Method Details

    • read

      public CompletableFuture<ParameterOutcome> read(PeerId target, String name)
      Reads one named parameter. Completes with ParameterOutcome.Status.NO_REPLY when the vehicle stays silent — which is also how an autopilot says "I have no such parameter": the protocol gives it no way to answer a name it does not recognise, so an unsupported parameter and an unreachable one are the same observation, and this service does not pretend otherwise.

    • readAll

      public CompletableFuture<Map<String,ParameterOutcome>> readAll(PeerId target, List<String> names)
      Reads several named parameters, all in flight at once — they occupy distinct MatchKeys, so they neither collide nor serialise, and one unanswered name costs the whole batch one timeout window rather than a place in a queue. Duplicates in names are collapsed (two live waiters on one key is an IllegalStateException by Correlator's own contract, and would be a caller-visible fault for a harmless input).

      The returned map is keyed by normalised name and preserves names' order. On a genuinely constrained link a caller should chunk rather than pass a list of hundreds: this method puts names.size() × (1 + retries) small packets on the air in the worst case.

    • write

      public CompletableFuture<ParameterOutcome> write(PeerId target, String name, float value, io.dronefleet.mavlink.common.MavParamType type)
      Writes one named parameter and verifies what the vehicle stored.
      Parameters:
      type - the vehicle's storage type for this parameter. ArduPilot ignores this field and uses its own table; PX4 does not, and a wrong type there is a rejected or mis-stored write — which is exactly what the read-back surfaces as ParameterOutcome.Status.MISMATCH rather than a silent success.
